title: The clock bug set for January 2038
summary: Unix time stored in a signed 32-bit integer overflows at 03:14:07 UTC on 19 January 2038.

beats.say: In twenty thirty eight, some computers will think it's nineteen oh one.
Many systems count time in seconds since January first, nineteen seventy.
That count is stored in a signed thirty two bit number.
One bit marks the sign. Thirty one bits hold the value.
The largest value it can hold is about two point one billion.
Two point one billion seconds is about sixty eight years.
Count sixty eight years from nineteen seventy and you land in twenty thirty eight.
One second later, the number wraps to a large negative value.
Systems that read it see December, nineteen oh one.
Switch to sixty four bits and the deadline moves two hundred ninety two billion years.
The fix exists. Old unpatched systems are the problem.
beats.cap: The fix exists. The old systems remain.

claims.note: Wikipedia: 03:14:07 UTC on 19 January 2038 is the last representable second; Hackaday gives the same moment
Wikipedia: Unix time stored as a signed 32-bit integer
Wikipedia: one second later the value overflows to -2^31, which systems read as 20:45:52 UTC on 13 December 1901
Wikipedia: a signed 64-bit integer pushes the wraparound out to about 292 billion years
Wikipedia: about 292 billion years to overflow

facts.claim: Unix time counts seconds from 00:00:00 UTC on 1 January 1970
facts.note: Wikipedia: 00:00:00 UTC on 1 January 1970, the Unix epoch

facts.claim: A signed 32-bit counter overflows after 2,147,483,647 seconds, at 03:14:07 UTC on 19 January 2038
facts.note: Hackaday: overflows at 03:14:07 UTC on January 19, 2038, 2,147,483,647 seconds after the epoch; wraps to -2,147,483,648

facts.claim: Older embedded and unpatched systems remain at risk, while modern 64-bit systems are largely fine
facts.note: Hackaday: unpatched software and older embedded or long-running systems are at risk; most modern 64-bit systems are fine
